name: Walungge
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Walungge is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Caplow 2009 (UCSB PhD on stress and Tibetan tonogenesis), is filed under walu1241 because Hammarström's record lists 'Tokpe Gola = Walungge [ola]' among its languages alongside Balti and Rebkong Amdo; no open copy exists (ProQuest preview only, no repository/Wayback/Google Books preview; Secondary descriptions (Bartram 2011, Caplow 2016 LTBA abstract, Tournadre & Suzuki 2023) present it as reconstructing Proto-Tibetan σ2 (non-verb) / σ1 (verb) stress from Balti and Rebkong Amdo, with σ2 H tone in tonal dialects as its reflex. The authoritative first-hand statement for Walungge itself is Bartram 2011 (SOAS PhD, already on file and read): acoustically established second-syllable stress on non-verbs, root (usually first-syllable) stress on verbs, and a minority of first-syllable-stressed nouns (pp. 209, 211, 256). new_statements.quote: In general, all polysyllabic non-verbs on their second syllable have a combination of greater duration, higher pitch, and greater intensity. For disyllabic words the differences between first and second syllable measurements for each of these acoustic parameters have been analysed statistically and are significant. These differences cannot simply be explained as correlates of high tone because they occur on the second syllable even when both the first and second syllables have high tone. The conclusion is that as a general pattern Walungge has second syllable stress for words which are not verbs. Verbs have stress on their root, which is in general the first syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the second syllable of polysyllabic non-verbs (nouns, adjectives, numerals), established instrumentally (duration, F0 maximum, intensity all greater on syllable 2, regardless of syllable weight and of the word's H/L tone). Verbs are stressed on the root, normally the first syllable; with the negative prefix ma- the stressed root is the second syllable. Walungge is also a word-tone language (one underlying H or L per word realised on syllable 1; syllable 2 always high, later syllables low), and the author argues tone is synchronically independent of stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; syllables after the second are described only as unfooted with low pitch.
new_statements.exceptions: A minority of nouns have first-syllable stress, e.g. [ˈtɕʰuwa] 'tap', [ˈʈʰukpa] 'sixth one' (p. 211; also 'a small handful of high tone nouns' p. 202); verbs stress the root (first syllable) rather than syllable 2; inflectional suffixes are extra-tonal/outside the tonal domain. A heavy (CVN) first syllable does not attract stress (p. 197).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; acoustic measurements on disyllabic words recorded in isolation/citation frames from four speakers (verbs vs. deverbal nouns in sentence frames, two speakers). Author notes sentence-final pitch always falls to low regardless of tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Bartram 2011 describes Walungge as spoken in Olangchung Gola (Walung/Halung), Yangma, Gunsa and Lungthung on the upper Tamur and Gunsa rivers, Taplejung District, NE Nepal (speakers from Lungthung, Olangchung Gola, Yangma, Gunsa, Kyabla). She treats Tokpe Gola Tibetan (Tokpe Gola, Shimbuk, Papung, Thudam on the upper Mewa; Caplow's field variety, Tournadre & Suzuki's 'Drogpa-kä') as a closely related, mutually intelligible variety but does not include it in her data; Glottolog groups both under walu1241. The Caplow works on the wishlist concern Tokpe Gola (and Balti/Amdo), not Olangchung Gola Walungge proper.

new_statements.reading: Walungge word stress is fixed on the second syllable for non-verbs (nouns, adjectives, numerals), counted from the left edge; verbs are stressed on the root, normally the first syllable (with the negative prefix ma- the root, hence σ2, is stressed); a lexical minority of nouns has first-syllable stress (e.g. 'tap', 'sixth one', p. 211). Stress is category-conditioned with lexical exceptions, not weight-sensitive, and independent of the fixed σ2 high tone. For a catalog coding: second-syllable (left-edge) stress as the dominant pattern, with a verb/non-verb split and lexical exceptions. (The extracted text layer renders hyphens as '3', e.g. 'non3verbs'; the quote restores the hyphen.)

Sec. 7.3.3 'Stress' (pp. 241-242) is family-level (Balti, Lhasa, Zhongu, mBalhag examples; cites Caplow 2009, 2016); sec. 7.3.4 says most tonal dialects have a trochaic pattern over the first two syllables. sources.citation: Bartram, Cathryn Virginia (2011). An investigation of tone in Walungge. PhD thesis, School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London. 375 pp. (not in the sweep's title list because the title lacks a stress keyword; it is the first-hand stress source)
sources.quote: p. 209: "The conclusion is that as a general pattern Walungge has second syllable stress for words which are not verbs. Verbs have stress on their root, which is in general the first syllable." p. 211: "although the typical pattern on nouns is second syllable stress, section 5.2 also shows that there are a minority of nouns which have first syllable stress, e.g. [ˈtɕʰuwa ⁴⁴ ⁴⁴] 'tap' [ˈʈʰukpa ¹¹ ⁴⁴] 'sixth one'". p. 256: "The acoustic analysis of stress patterns showed that in general Walungge has second syllable stress ... synchronically tone is independent of stress in as much as the second syllable of a polysyllabic word has high tone regardless of whether the word has the prevailing second syllable stress pattern or whether the word is one of the minority of words which have first syllable stress."
sources.locator: sec. 5.2 'Acoustic analysis of stress in Walungge', pp. 192-209; conclusion sec. 5.2.6 p. 209 (PDF 210); sec. 5.3.2 p. 211 (PDF 212); ch. 5 summary p. 256 (PDF 257)
sources.note: Acoustic study (duration, F0 max, intensity; statistically significant σ1 vs σ2 differences in disyllables): non-verbs (nouns, adjectives, numerals) carry stress on the second syllable as the general pattern; verbs are stressed on the root, in general the first syllable (negative prefix ma- + root puts stress on the root = σ2); a lexical minority of nouns has first-syllable stress. Stress is category-conditioned and lexically exceptional, not weight-driven; independent of the σ2 H tone that all polysyllabic content words carry (tonal foot over the first two syllables).

sources.quote: hh record, lgcode = {Balti (Baltistan-northern Pakistan), Rebkong Amdo = Amdo Tibetan [adx], Tokpe Gola = Walungge [ola]}. Google Books fragment: "The prominent F0 reconstructed for sigma2 of Proto-Tibetan nouns accounts for constraints on tone patterns long-observed and long-unexplained in the geographically central dialects. There, tone on sigma1 can be either L or H, but tone on sigma2 can only be H. I offer a new explanation for this sigma2 H tone: it is an acoustic reflex of Proto-Tibetan stress." Bartram 2011 p. 191: "Caplow (2009) considers the second-syllable-high tone patterns of Tibetan languages in the light of the stress patterns found in two Tibetan languages which have been described as being atonal. In particular she looks at stress in Balti and in Rebkong Amdo Tibetan ... In both these languages, disyllabic nouns, adjectives, and numerals have second syllable stress."
